It always pays to keep one's ears free of wax, as one never knows when one is going to overhear some titbit of information that later proves invaluable. Such was the case at the Dionysus Club, yesterday afternoon, when you happened to overhear the noted psychiatrist, Doctor Cornelius Drake, he of the ginger moustache, talking over the phone to his secretary.

"Cancel all my appointments for tomorrow, Miss Henshaw," said the shrink, "I've been summoned down to Hamcestershire by the Earl of Hamcester. Never met the fellow, but he'd heard of me by reputation.  Wants me to give his brother-in-law the once-over. Apparently, the poor chap thinks he's exploring the Congo. Sounds like a clear case of incorrigible delusion to me."

This telephone communication piqued your interest, and the reason it piqued your interest was that you happened to know that the Lord Hamcester to whom it referred was a collector of sorts, and that amongst his collection was an extremely valuable Egyptian jewelled scarab. In fact he had outbid you at auction for the very piece. It is a sad fact that amateur collectors are rarely aware of the true value of the pieces they possess, and it is not uncommon to find them displayed among a plethora of inferior items. Who knows what other gems might be squirrelled away amongst the bric-a-brac at Bunkham Hall?

It was the work of a moment to call Miss Henshaw, posing as the Earl, and cancel the appointment. And it was an equally simple matter, the following morning, to don a suitable disguise and take the 10.15 to St Bartholomew-on-the-Bog, Hamcestershire, in Doctor Drake's place. All in a day's work for Sir Rodney Playfair, alias the notorious gentleman thief known as "The Magpie"!

Alias 'The Magpie'
An interactive caper by J. J. Guest
Release 5 / Serial number 220210 / Inform 7 build 6M62 (I6/v6.33 lib 6/12N) 
(Type "about" for credits and game information.)

Lord Hamcester's Study
A small, cosy study, impeccably neat, with walnut panelling and a leather-topped desk of a similar complexion. There are a few homely touches; a framed newspaper clipping and a photograph hang on the wall beside you. A sturdy wooden chair faces the desk. The door, leading south into the library, is closed.

A ghastly amateur watercolour hangs above the desk.

On the walnut desk is a pamphlet.

Lord Hamcester regards you haughtily from behind his desk.

"Good of you to come at such short notice, Doctor," says Lord Hamcester. "You've read my telegram I take it?"

(You could say yes or no, if you liked.)

 Lord Hamcester's Study
 Exits: SOUTH

"I see, so you'd like me to go incognito, as it were?" you say, winking.

"That's the ticket. I've told her you're the famous Belgian detective chappie, Hermes Perroquet. He's a member of my club, and my wife's been on at me to invite him over for ages. Can't stand the fellow myself, but the wife's dotty about detective stories, so if you happen to run into her, just play along, there's a good chap. events.intent: Step into the great hall, triggering the Perroquet eavesdropping scene
events.response:
No sooner have you stepped into the great hall, than you have stepped back out again, for there is someone in the great hall whom you would really rather wasn't there. In fact, if all the people you could wish to be there were ranked in order of preference, this particular person would be right at the bottom of the list. It is the great detective, Hermes Perroquet.  You notice, with growing consternation, that the great detective is in conference with the very last person you could wish him to be in conference with, namely, Lady Hamcester. But the "Magpie's" feathers are rarely ruffled. Keeping out of sight behind the door of the library, you listen with interest to their conversation:

"I'm sorry, I didn't catch your name. Hives rather gave the impression that it was Hermes Perroquet."

"Your butler was quite correct, Madame, I am Hermes Perroquet."

"But that's impossible."

"Madame?"

"You can't be Hermes Perroquet. Hermes Perroquet is a guest at this house. He has been here all afternoon."

"Madame, I assure you, that is who I am. I have been sent here to investigate the sighting of a gorilla near the grounds of your house this morning by a neighbour of yours, a Mrs Croup, housekeeper at Bunkham Manor."

"A gorilla?"

"Yes, Madame."

"I am not in the mood for practical jokes, Monsieur Whoever-You-Are. There are no gorillas anywhere in or around the grounds of Bunkham Hall. Gorillas, I think you'll find, live in the jungles of Africa, not in rural Hamcestershire."

"But Madame, I assure you..."

"I don't know who put you up to this, but if I were to hazard a guess, I'd say it was Sir Humphrey Leghorn. If this is a ruse to get at my husband's cucumber, then you ought to have come up with a better one. Gorillas, indeed!"

The great detective embarks upon another sentence, beginning again with the word "Madame," but that is as far as he gets, since Lady Hamcester has slammed the door in his face. With a sharp "tsk", she trots off in the direction of the terrace.

Collection Room
This small, oak-panelled room serves as sort of miniature museum for Lord Hamcester's collection of objets d'art, if one can use that term. Objets d'ordures might better describe the grotesque items residing on plinths around the perimeter of the collection room. Still, even the most inept collector occasionally gets lucky.

The collection room is dominated by a glass display case in the centre. The items contained there are, presumably, the most valuable.  The display case is currently closed, and locked.

From here, the only exit leads east, into the saloon.

"A few weeks ago my husband bought a jewelled scarab thingy at auction," says Lady Hamcester, indicating the glass display cabinet in front of you. "It was the pride of his collection. This morning I came in here and lo and behold, the bally thing's gone walkies. Fortunately, he's been holed up in his office all morning working on a speech, but if he finds out it's missing, he'll blow a fuse. He's bound to blame it on poor Hilary."

"I see, Madame," you say, "You would like me to find zis, zis scarab then?"

"I know it's a frightful liberty, since you're a guest here."

"Not at all Madame! Not at all! The great Hermes Perroquet is always on duty!"

"I say," says the Countess suddenly, grabbing your arm, "you don't think this could be the work of the notorious 'Magpie', do you?"

"Hmm. Could be, Madame, could be. The 'Magpie' is a very cunning, and some say very charming and handsome fellow."

"Very well then, I'll leave you to it. Keep me posted, and don't let on." The Countess winks and taps her nose, before stepping off in the direction of the terrace.

Well, this complicates things somewhat. You turn up at a place to steal something, only to find that someone's beaten you to it. But you came here to pinch it, and pinch it you will! There's no sign of forced entry. Whoever stole that scarab opened the display case with a key. It has all the hallmarks of an inside job, and you'd bet your last penny that the scarab is still in the house somewhere. The question is, where?

You follow Lady Hamcester into the collection room.

Collection Room
This small, oak-panelled room serves as sort of miniature museum for Lord Hamcester's collection of objets d'art, if one can use that term. Objets d'ordures might better describe the grotesque items residing on plinths around the perimeter of the collection room. Still, even the most inept collector occasionally gets lucky.

The collection room is dominated by a glass display case in the centre. The items contained there are, presumably, the most valuable.  The display case is currently closed, and locked.

From here, the only exit leads east, into the saloon.

"A few weeks ago my husband bought a jewelled scarab thingy at auction," says Lady Hamcester, indicating the glass display cabinet in front of you. "It was the pride of his collection. This morning I came in here and lo and behold, the bally thing's gone walkies. Fortunately, he's been holed up in his office all morning working on a speech, but if he finds out it's missing, he'll blow a fuse. He's bound to blame it on poor Hilary."

"I see, Madame," you say, "You would like me to find zis, zis scarab then?"

"I know it's a frightful liberty, since you're a guest here."

"Not at all Madame! Not at all! The great Hermes Perroquet is always on duty!"

"I say," says the Countess suddenly, grabbing your arm, "you don't think this could be the work of the notorious 'Magpie', do you?"

"Hmm. Could be, Madame, could be. The 'Magpie' is a very cunning, and some say very charming and handsome fellow."

"Very well then, I'll leave you to it. Keep me posted, and don't let on." The Countess winks and taps her nose, before stepping off in the direction of the terrace.

Well, this complicates things somewhat. You turn up at a place to steal something, only to find that someone's beaten you to it. But you came here to pinch it, and pinch it you will! There's no sign of forced entry. Whoever stole that scarab opened the display case with a key. It has all the hallmarks of an inside job, and you'd bet your last penny that the scarab is still in the house somewhere. The question is, where?

 Collection Room
 Exits: east

There are generally two types of collector; those who strew their objets d'art about the place willy-nilly, and the fastidious type who prefer their antiquities arranged according to category. Lord Hamcester is of the latter variety, but the meticulous mind is all too often lacking in artistic taste, and the best that can be said for most of these objets is that they're very neatly organised. events.intent: Step out onto the west balcony
events.response:
You step out into the bright sunshine.

West Balcony
The balcony offers splendid views of the park and grounds. From here you can see into the kitchen garden, to the left of which is a wide expanse of lawn. French windows lead into the blue room. A ladder leans against the balustrade.

A sturdy-looking cast iron drainpipe runs down the wall beside the balcony.

As you step out onto the balcony, you are mildly perturbed to see that the ladder is no longer where you left it. Hearing voices on the terrace below, you duck down behind the balustrade in order to watch unobserved. Through a gap in the ivy, you are able to see the under-gardener, holding the ladder, in conversation with Lord Hamcester, who appears to have taken a break from ordering Hives around in order to enjoy a cigar.

"What was it doing there?" says Hamcester.

"I don't know, sir," says the under-gardener, shuffling his feet nervously. "I saw the gentleman carrying it over from the orchard, sir, and there it was."

"The gentleman? Are you referring to, er, ah, our guest?"

"The gentleman with the ginger moustache, sir."

"I see. So you're telling me that you observed the gentleman with the ginger moustache carry the ladder from the orchard towards the house, and lean it up against the balcony?"

"Well, yes, sir. I mean, no sir."

"Yes, no? Which is it, man? You're blithering."

"I mean to say I saw him, the gentleman with the moustache, sir, carry the ladder from the orchard, but I didn't see him lean it up against the balcony, sir, on account of being unable to see the balcony from where I was situated, sir."

"I see. Odd, dashed odd. Very good, Boyle. Don't let that ladder out of your sight. There's some funny business going on at Bunkham Hall today, and I shouldn't be at all surprised if Sir Humphrey Leghorn were at the bottom of it."

Tucking the ladder under his arm, the under-gardener sets off around the side of the kitchen-garden. Hamcester, meanwhile, gazes across from the west balcony to the top of the kitchen-garden wall, as though trying to judge whether it would be possible to jump from one to the other. Shaking his head, he retires into the house.

 West Balcony
 Exits: north inside

Bunkham Hall's grandest room has become a scene of devastation to rival the ruins of Pompeii. Drive
Bunkham Hall began life as a modest country house in the Jacobean style. In 1768, the fourth Earl of Hamcester had it remodelled by Robert Addams, a jobbing builder with no architectural training who traded rather lucratively on the reputation of his talented near-namesake Robert Adam. Whereas Adam's buildings are noted for their elegant proportions and scrupulous attention to detail, Addams's by contrast are noted for their inelegant proportions and tendency to collapse if you so much as look askance at them. It's amazing the house has lasted this long.

At first glance, Bunkham Hall is a pleasant enough example of Eighteenth Century neoclassicism, but the more one looks, the less harmonious it appears in its general proportions. The façade is asymmetrical, the scalloped Rococo window frames totally out of keeping. The ionic portico, beneath which the front door leads inwards, is much too squat, and appears to be listing to one side.

Here begins the long driveway that doesn't so much connect the Hall with the village to the north as keep it at a safe distance.

Saloon
Bunkham Hall's grandest room has become a scene of devastation to rival the ruins of Pompeii.  Barely a stick of furniture remains intact, and Hamcester's hideous collection of porcelain lies in fragments on the floor. The Axminster carpet is decorated with a delicate pattern of daisies and fragrant, steaming cowpats. To the north and east are the great hall and the dining room respectively. events.intent: Step through the French windows onto the terrace
events.response:
You step out into the bright sunshine.

Terrace
A charming terrace, surrounded by an Italian balustrade, and replete with statues of dancing fauns, ornamental urns and what-not. In the centre is a set of cast-iron garden furniture, doing what cast-iron garden furniture does best.

Stone steps lead southwards onto the lawn, east and west to the gravel sweep, whilst to the north French windows invite you to enter the saloon.

Lady Hamcester sits on a cast-iron garden chair leafing through a brochure for the R.M.S. Aquitania.

Standing beside the countess is a rather dishevelled Hives. He bears, in his twiglike arms, a silver tray, about which are buzzing a number of wasps. "I regret to report that dinner will be delayed indefinitely, Madam," says the butler, "owing to a mishap in the dining room."

"Not another mishap, Hives?"

"Yes, madam. Bread and treacle is the best I am able to offer, your Ladyship, until a replacement set of tableware can be located."

But before the butler can dish up the comestibles, a wild figure jumps out from behind a statue of a prancing faun. It is the Major, brandishing a slingshot of gigantic proportions.

"Japanese hornets!" he cries. "Beastly devils. Stand back, I'm a dead shot!" Leaping up onto the balustrade, the Major pulls back the elastic and lets fly a large stone. The projectile misses the wasps, but hits the tin of treacle square-on. The badly dented tin sails end-over-end, before clattering to the flagstones not far from your feet, where the treacle oozes into a large puddle.

"I think you had better cancel bread and treacle, too, Hives," says Lady Hamcester. The butler sighs, and retreats into the house, followed by the Major.

 Terrace

events.intent: See the aftermath of the Major's catharsis and whether he is cured
events.response:
Music Room
This modestly proportioned music room, located north of the drawing room, has a somewhat neglected feel, and is almost entirely bereft of musical instruments. This is not altogether surprising; Lord Hamcester is regarded throughout the London club scene as something of a "wet blanket". Where once stood a fine concert grand, there now lies a large heap of wreckage.

An alcove, originally intended to be occupied by an organ, instead contains a small mahogany side table, on which are a framed photograph and a gramophone. The hotch-potch of furniture also includes a sagging Victorian day-bed and a green tub chair.

Languishing soggily in the middle of the floor is one half of Shenandoah, Lord Hamcester's prize cucumber. The other half has passed beyond identification.

Red-faced with rage, the Major is bashing merry hell out of the grand piano with a medieval mace.

Over in the alcove, a gramophone record entitled Maraca Medley is playing.

His work completed, the Major stops, drops the mace and staggering from the exertion, suddenly sags. He gazes with incomprehension at the devastation and whispers "Oh, Woody! Dear Woody." Then, as though a stage hypnotist had snapped his fingers, the Major gives a start, straightens, and stares around him as though through brand new eyes.

"Well well, old Bunkham Hall!" he says. "My word! However did I come to be here? Old Emerick's let the place go a bit." Suddenly he appears to notice you. "Hullo! I don't believe we've been introduced. Major Hilary Buff-Orpington."

This puts you in a bit of a spot, an introduction being, for you, a multiple-choice question. But before you have time to reply there is a clatter of feet as Lord Hamcester skids into the room, his eyes fixed on the destroyed piano.

"That was a priceless Steinway!" he bellows.

"Not any more," you reply, but suddenly the matter of the piano seems to have slipped entirely from his Lordship's mind, for he has noticed the half a cucumber lying in the middle of the floor. Perhaps sensing danger ahead, the Major slips unnoticed from the room, pausing only to pluck a green carnation from a bowl on the sideboard and tuck it into his lapel.

events.response:
Music Room

An alcove, originally intended to be occupied by an organ, instead contains a small mahogany side table, on which are a framed photograph and a gramophone. The hotch-potch of furniture also includes a sagging Victorian day-bed and a green tub chair.

Lord Hamcester is standing in the centre of the room, staring at the wreckage of Shenandoah, his prize cucumber. The expression he wears might best be described by the adjective 'aghast', or possibly 'agog', or even 'agape'.

Languishing soggily in the middle of the floor is one half of Shenandoah, Lord Hamcester's prize cucumber. The other half has passed beyond identification.

The gramophone stops playing.

Lord Hamcester drops to his knees and begins to run his hands through his sparse hair, setting it in disarray.

"Oh, no, no!" he cries, "Oh, Shenandoah! Oh, the humanity!" He jumps to his feet suddenly and lunges towards you, grabbing you by the lapels. "This is all your fault, you and your so-called psychology!"

"You seem a trifle distraught, your Lordship," you reply, soothingly. "Perhaps a lie down on the couch would do you good?"

The earl seems to take your advice to heart and flings himself down on the Victorian day-bed, where he begins to moan, softly. Well, well, a chance to play psychiatrist, for real! How wonderfully diverting.

events.intent: Cross to the great hall
events.response:
No sooner have you stepped into the great hall, than you have stepped back out again, for there is someone in the great hall whom you would really rather wasn't there. In fact, if all the people you could wish to be there were ranked in order of preference, this particular person would be right at the bottom of the list. It is the great detective, Hermes Perroquet.  You notice, with growing consternation, that the great detective is in conference with the very last person you could wish him to be in conference with, namely, Lady Hamcester. But the "Magpie's" feathers are rarely ruffled. Keeping out of sight behind the door of the library, you listen with interest to their conversation:

"I'm sorry, I didn't catch your name. Hives rather gave the impression that it was Hermes Perroquet."

"Your butler was quite correct, Madame, I am Hermes Perroquet."

"But that's impossible."

"Madame?"

"You can't be Hermes Perroquet. Hermes Perroquet is a guest at this house. He has been here all afternoon."

"Madame, I assure you, that is who I am. I have been sent here to investigate the sighting of a gorilla near the grounds of your house this morning by a neighbour of yours, a Mrs Croup, housekeeper at Bunkham Manor."

"A gorilla?"

"Yes, Madame."

"I am not in the mood for practical jokes, Monsieur Whoever-You-Are. There are no gorillas anywhere in or around the grounds of Bunkham Hall. Gorillas, I think you'll find, live in the jungles of Africa, not in rural Hamcestershire."

"But Madame, I assure you..."

"I don't know who put you up to this, but if I were to hazard a guess, I'd say it was Sir Humphrey Leghorn. If this is a ruse to get at my husband's cucumber, then you ought to have come up with a better one. Gorillas, indeed!"

The great detective embarks upon another sentence, beginning again with the word "Madame," but that is as far as he gets, since Lady Hamcester has slammed the door in his face. With a sharp "tsk", she trots off in the direction of the terrace.

events.intent: Enter the folly

The Folly
The interior of the folly, insofar as you can see it given the limited light admitted by the open door, is pretty spartan for an Athenian temple. There are faded frescoes on the walls depicting scenes from Greek antiquity, but for the most part the building is given over to the storage of equipment used in the maintenance of the gardens. Where might have stood statues of Greek gods, now stand rusted lawn rollers. Where once had sat Grecian urns, now are empty paint tins and upturned planters.

Sitting in the middle of the floor, moaning softly and rubbing its head, is a gorilla.

The Major is standing by the door, staring in a dreamy sort of way at the gorilla, as though wondering where he'd seen it before.

A large, battered can sits in the corner of the folly, its label turned to the wall.

You can also see a banana here.

"Oh, my head," says the gorilla, blinking in the light from the open door. "Who the devil are you?"

"My name is Hermes Perroquet," you reply. "I have the reputation of being Belgium's greatest detective, and at the present time, I am on the trail of the notorious jewel thief known as the 'Magpie'. It is in this capacity that I find myself obliged to ask, who the devil are you, and why are you sneaking around Bunkham Hall disguised as a gorilla?"

"Good gracious!" says the gorilla, giving a start. "You don't think — you don't think I'm the 'Magpie', do you?"

events.intent: Answer no — I do not think the gorilla is the Magpie

"Non, Monsieur, I do not believe you are the 'Magpie'. I believe you are Sir Humphrey Leghorn, of Bunkham Manor. But perhaps you would like to explain to me, why you are locked in the folly at Bunkham Hall, disguised as an ape?"

"It's all perfectly simple," says the gorilla, flustered. "Tomorrow is the St Bartholomew-on-the-Bog annual Village Fête cucumber growing competition. Every year Lord Hamcester wins by a country mile, and I'm convinced he's cheating. I wanted to find out for certain, but I couldn't just walk in and start nosing around. That blasted under-gardener is watching the place day and night. But then I read in the paper about that escaped gorilla, and it gave me an idea."

"So, you disguised yourself as an ape, yes?"

"Exactly! I ran up to London and bought a gorilla suit, thinking I could use it to scare off the under-gardener and take a look inside Hamcester's kitchen garden, but before I could get anywhere near it, the Major here snuck up behind me and bopped me over the head."

"Terribly sorry, old bean," says the Major, "Thought you were the real deal. Haven't been feeling myself just lately."

"I've been here ever since, subsisting on bananas."

Barely a stick of furniture remains intact, and Hamcester's hideous collection of porcelain lies in fragments on the floor. The Axminster carpet is decorated with a delicate pattern of daisies and fragrant, steaming cowpats. To the north and east are the great hall and the dining room respectively. The collection room lies to the west, whilst to the south, the remains of some French windows open onto the terrace.

Her ladyship stands amongst the broken porcelain, staring wildly. She retreats hurriedly into the collection room.

Hives stands transfixed in the middle of the Saloon, looking like a startled rabbit. He turns around and heads into the great hall.

events.intent: North to the country lane
events.response:
Country Lane
A narrow country lane connecting the village, to the east, with the railway station, to the west. You walked along it only this morning, and a very pleasant walk it was too. To the north are tall hedgerows, behind which are presumably fields of some sort, whilst to the south, via the drive, lies Bunkham Hall. The chimney of what can only be Bunkham Manor, home of Sir Humphrey Leghorn, can be seen protruding from the hedges to the east.

Prodding perfunctorily about in the hedgerow, meanwhile, is Constable Cramp, of Scotland Yard. Presumably, he is looking for the tell-tale footprint of the lowland gorilla. Nestled under the Constable's arm is one of those guns that fire tranquiliser darts.

Pacing up and down the lane, with a neat, black moustache and a look of extreme vexation on his face, is that scourge of gentleman thieves, Hermes Perroquet.

A Black Maria is parked at the edge of the lane, with two wheels on the road and two in the long grass bordering the hedge.

Monsieur Perroquet gives a start as he sees you lumbering down the drive.

"There it is — le gorille!" he cries. "Quickly, constable, the tranquilliser gun!" 

The terrified constable fumbles with the tranquilliser gun, dropping it with a clatter, and picking it up again without one.

"Vite, vite!" says Perroquet, disarranging his perfectly lacquered hair in frustration.

 Country Lane
 Exits: south WEST

Constable Cramp puffs along behind the great detective, still fumbling with his tranquilizer gun.

"Now, constable," barks Perroquet. "It's getting away!"
